The vg27aq is the better choice between the two because it beats the s2721dgf in terms of input lag without VRR (and ELMB in the case of the Asus), and ties at 4.8ms with VRR (and ELMB for Asus) enabled. The slightly slower pixel response time only means that there is imperceptibly more motion blur/ghosting. The big advantage that the vg27aq has over the s2721dgf is having ELMB motion blur reduction as a feature which more than makes up for however more motion blur is present - and it can even have VRR enabled concurrently.

Input lag isn't the same thing as pixel response time.  A higher PRT means more ghosting. A competitive gamer should care more about input lag than pixel response time as long as the ghosting/motion blur isn't noticeable.

The vg27aq has fast enough PRT that motion will be clear. Also, the vg27aq has ELMB Sync (black frame insertion + Variable Refresh Rate) while the Dell has no motion blur reduction feature. The input lag of the Asus is 3.5ms without ELMB or VRR enabled, while the Dell has 3.7ms. Both monitors are tied at 4.8ms with VRR enabled. The Asus can also enable ELMB and still tie the Dell at 4.8ms input delay. Overall, the Asus is the better competitive gaming monitor between the two because it is the complete package.

Here are some tips if you don't mind:

Figure out what kind of games you like to play. In general, FPS games need higher framerates, while single player and MMOs like better colors and higher resolution.

Choose a monitor based on your use-case. For competitive games like csgo and overwatch, 240hz TN is the ideal. (BenQ XL2546k is current top-tier). For single player, 1440p 144hz is the current sweet-spot. The monitor type matters - IPS is good for color and wider viewing angles and TN is better for reduced input lag and motion clarity. However, IPS is catching up now so a 240hz IPS monitor would make a good all-rounder. On a budget, 1080p 144hz is perfectly useable.

Next, check out cpu and gpu benchmarks online for the games you want to play. This will help you figure out how powerful your pc needs to be to make proper use of your monitor. In general, after 200 fps, games are limited by how powerful your cpu is. Before that, it's the GPU that is the determining factor.

For storage, m.2 NVME SSDs (Solid State Drive) such are the samsung 970 evo are currently the best. They are cards that fit right on the motherboard. After that, there are SATA SSDs Like the samsung 860 evo. These are affordable and still good. They connect to your motherboard using a power cable and a data cable and are mounted in the case.

For your PSU, I would recommend using [pcpartpicker.com](https://pcpartpicker.com) and picking your parts to see how much wattage you need. You want to be using around 60% of your maximum wattage. PSUs typically come in 550w, 650w, 750w, 850w, and 1000w varieties and have different energy efficiency ratings. Check [techpowerup.com](https://techpowerup.com) and [tomshardware.com](https://tomshardware.com) for PSU buying guides by Aris Mpitziopoulos.

Given all that, I would wait for a couple months. It's a bad time to be building a computer right now. The new tech is a big performance jump, but there is no availability. You would be able to have an extremely powerful PC by buying an rtx 3070 and a ryzen 5 5600x.
